query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser shock peening (LSP) applied to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will generate beneficial compressive residual stresses and a near‐surface grain refinement that improves the alloy’s load‐bearing integrity (i.e., increases fracture toughness and reduces crack propagation) while preserving its intrinsic field‐ and pressure‐induced caloric responses.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy showing large reversible caloric effects but with poor load-bearing integrity and a tendency to crack under load.
generation.intervention: Apply laser shock peening (LSP) to the alloy surface under controlled parameters.
generation.conditions: Testing under operating conditions typical for solid refrigeration (fields and pressures used to induce the caloric effect, with operational temperatures near the caloric phase transformation) and under mechanical load conditions representative of service requirements.
generation.structural_mediator: Induced near-surface compressive residual stresses and slight grain refinement (or modified grain-boundary structure) that inhibit microcrack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: LSP introduces a compressive stress layer and refines or reconfigures near-surface microstructures without substantially altering the bulk phase that mediates the caloric transformation. The compressive stresses counteract tensile stresses at flaws and crack tips, thereby increasing resistance to mechanical failure while maintaining the reversible phase transformation that gives rise to the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in fracture toughness and fatigue life (e.g., an improvement in load-bearing integrity by at least 10–15%) with caloric performance (entropy change, temperature span) retained within ±5% of the untreated state.
generation.baseline: The untreated alloy displays a strong caloric response but suffers from cracking and poor mechanical integrity under load.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected in the treated near-surface region (up to ~100 μm depth) and within the field, pressure, and temperature regimes employed in current refrigeration applications. Excessive LSP energy could potentially alter bulk phase behavior, so the treatment window must be carefully optimized.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends evidence from studies where thermo-mechanical treatments (e.g., cryo-rolling with annealing in PMC5818523 and grain-boundary serration in PMC9848264) improved mechanical integrity without detrimental effects on functional properties. The novel aspect here is applying LSP—a non-thermal, mechanical surface treatment—to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 system. Uncertainty remains on possible subsurface phase changes due to shock loading; preliminary parameter studies will be needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38: one set treated with optimized laser shock peening (LSP) and one untreated control. Perform mechanical tests (e.g., tensile, bending, and fatigue crack propagation testing) alongside in-situ caloric measurements (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change) under the standard applied-field and pressure-field conditions.
measurements: Residual stress profiling (using X-ray diffraction or similar methods)
Microstructural characterization (via TEM/EBSD, focusing on grain size and grain-boundary features near the surface)
Mechanical properties (fracture toughness, fatigue life, tensile strength)
Caloric effect metrics (entropy change, temperature span) under field and pressure cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the LSP-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 10–15% increase) in load-bearing integrity or if the caloric response deviates by more than ±5% compared to the untreated alloy (or if undesirable phase transformations are induced), then the hypothesis is falsified.

This work has demonstrated that a simple post heat treatment could induce SEGB in a HEA fabricated by SLM. The serrations on grain boundary in HT-samples were attributed to the blocky irregular shaped γ′ precipitates formed during the slow cooling process, and they could pin the mobile grain boundaries as well as restricting grain growth, this phenomenon is known as the Zener drag effect []. The drag force from the coarse precipitates would hinder the migration of grain boundary, while those free from the precipitates could break free around the precipitates and resulted in serrated morphology (Figure 4(c)). The inhibition of grain growth from coarse precipitates explained why HT-2 sample possessed a smaller grain size than that of HT-1 sample. The difference in tensile yield strength between HT-1 and HT-2 at 25°C and 650°C could be associated with the size of γ′ precipitates. According to Jackson – Reed model [], the strengthening contribution of γ′ precipitate could be inverse proportional to the average radius of the precipitate.
